result.question: State of the art (July 2026) in AI coding-agent governance and harness design: instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), lifecycle hooks, deterministic verification gates, persistent memory across sessions/compaction, behavioral guardrails, git-level enforcement, task contracts, and parallel multi-agent orchestration — surveying Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, xAI, Chinese labs (Moonshot, Zhipu, DeepSeek, Tencent, MiniMax, Qwen), and independents (Nous Research, Fundamental Research Labs, the 'Ornith-1.0' team, tinygrad, OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin), to identify consensus, divergences, and citable insights for a 2026 rewrite of a drop-in governance kit; flag any named entity that cannot be verified.

results.title: Best practices for Claude Code — Anthropic official docs
results.snippet: Anthropic's canonical prescription for CLAUDE.md: keep it minimal and universally applicable (~150-200 instruction budget for frontier LLMs, ~50 already consumed by the system prompt, so target under ~300 lines), recommended top-to-bottom structure (project one-liner, stack, exact commands, 3-5 key directories, conventions, boundaries), what NOT to include (never send an LLM to do a linter's job), plus guidance on hooks for deterministic enforcement and subagents for context isolation. The single most load-bearing primary source for the governance-kit rewrite.

results.title: Custom instructions with AGENTS.md — OpenAI Codex official guide
results.snippet: OpenAI's official spec for AGENTS.md discovery and layering: CODEX_HOME-level AGENTS.override.md vs AGENTS.md, root-to-cwd directory walk with per-directory overrides, fallback filenames, and the fact that the merged file is concatenated into context at session start (inspectable via --print-instructions in 2026 CLI versions). Defines the cross-vendor instruction-file layering model a drop-in kit must interoperate with.

results.title: Provide context with GEMINI.md files — Gemini CLI official docs
results.snippet: Google's official GEMINI.md documentation: hierarchical loading (global ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, workspace and parent directories), concatenation into every prompt, @file.md modular imports, /memory show and /memory reload inspection commands, and memory routing (shared repo instructions vs private per-project notes vs global preferences) — Google's answer to persistent memory and instruction-file structure.

results.title: AGENTS.md — open cross-vendor specification
results.snippet: The official AGENTS.md spec, now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation directed fund) and supported by Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Claude Code (as fallback). Evidence of the convergent consensus around a single vendor-neutral instruction file — directly informs whether the governance kit should target CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, or both.

results.title: Agent SDK overview — Anthropic official docs
results.snippet: Anthropic's official Agent SDK docs covering the programmatic tool loop, lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop/SessionStart/SessionEnd/UserPromptSubmit) as deterministic callbacks that validate, block, or transform agent behavior, plus subagent context isolation and the memory tool for cross-session persistence — the vendor-official basis for prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement and hook-based verification gates.

results.title: Writing a good CLAUDE.md — HumanLayer
results.snippet: Widely cited independent (non-vendor but rigorous) treatment of CLAUDE.md authoring that popularized the instruction-count budget framing and the agent_docs/ pointer pattern; useful as the practitioner counterpart to Anthropic's official page when calibrating instruction-file length and structure for the kit.

results.title: From Conductor to Orchestrator: A Practical Guide to Multi-Agent Coding in 2026
results.snippet: 2026 practitioner guide that directly frames the orchestrator-worker pattern (Anthropic's lead-agent/subagent design, subagents with self-contained briefs and no peer awareness) against Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' critique, concluding both are right for different workloads — parallel research vs. tightly interdependent coding. Also covers native worktree support in Claude Code (v2.1.49+) and subagent decomposition with explicit file ownership. Ideal synthesis of the exact Anthropic-vs-Cognition tension the research question asks about.

results.title: The Code Agent Orchestra — what makes multi-agent coding work (Addy Osmani)
results.snippet: Respected independent engineering-leadership take on what actually makes multi-agent coding work: multiplicative gains from parallelism (~3x throughput), specialization (focused context), git-worktree isolation to prevent conflicts, and critic committees used as pre-submission gates and completion review. Surfaced in both the orchestration and adversarial-review searches, making it a strong cross-cutting citation for a governance-kit rewrite.

results.title: GitHub Copilot app: The agent-native desktop experience (GitHub Blog)
results.snippet: Official Microsoft/GitHub source (Build 2026, June 2) on how Copilot now structures multi-agent workflows: a desktop control plane ('mission control' / My Work view) where every agent session runs in its own isolated git worktree so agents work the same repo in parallel without clobbering each other, plus a GA Copilot SDK for embedding planner/tool loops, /fleet-style orchestrator-dispatched sub-agents, and AGENTS.md as the project instruction convention. Primary evidence for the Microsoft column of the comparison.

results.title: Adversarial Code Review pattern (ASDLC.io)
results.snippet: Pattern-catalog writeup of adversarial review for agentic coding: version-controlled reviewer prompts spawned as SDK subagents emitting structured JSON, so critics act as standardized functions inside build pipelines. Directly citable prescription for the adversarial-review + deterministic-gate half of the governance kit.

results.title: How to Use Git Worktrees for Parallel AI Agent Execution (Augment Code)
results.snippet: Concrete how-to on worktree isolation as the foundation of parallel agent execution: lightweight checkouts giving each agent its own working directory and branch without repo duplication, preventing merge conflicts during concurrent work. Vendor blog but substantive; useful for the worktree-isolation mechanics section (pairs with their multi-agent-workspace guide covering explicit task boundaries and evidence-based merges).

results.title: Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery (arXiv)
results.snippet: Research paper formalizing adversarial stage-gating: agents tasked with disproving findings, a cross-model critic for orthogonal error detection, and mandatory empirical validation as the final gate. Key citable findings for the prompt-vs-deterministic-enforcement debate: agent consensus does not equal correctness (80+ agents unanimously endorsed a non-existent vulnerability), and LLM critics are systematically weak at 'DO NOT' constraint violations without deterministic gate backing.

results.title: Harness Engineering for Coding Agent Users (Birgitta Böckeler, martinfowler.com, Apr 2026)
results.snippet: Canonical 2026 practitioner framing: Agent = Model + Harness; prescribes 'enforce quality with mechanisms, not prompts' — LLM instruction compliance is probabilistic, so rules files must be backed by deterministic gates (linters, hooks, CI), pushed to the fastest layer (PostToolUse hook > pre-commit > CI > human review). Directly citable for prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement in a governance kit.

results.title: Inside the Scaffold: A Source-Code Taxonomy of Coding Agent Architectures (arXiv, 2026)
results.snippet: Reads the actual source of Claude Code, Codex CLI, Aider, Cline, OpenHands, SWE-agent and taxonomizes harness design: agent loop, tool interface, context management (compaction + tool-output offloading), and control mechanisms. Documents that persistent memory ranges from nonexistent (benchmark agents) to multi-tier pipelines (interactive agents) — the exact comparative evidence base the survey needs.

results.title: OpenHands Context Condenser (official SDK docs)
results.snippet: Concrete compaction-survival engineering from a leading open harness: event-store architecture with nine pluggable condenser strategies (heuristic vs LLM-based), keeping recent messages intact while summaries preserve user goals, progress, critical files, and failing tests — a citable reference design for persisting working state across compaction.

results.title: Cline Memory Bank: How to Make Cline an AI Agent That Never Forgets
results.snippet: The influential open-source pattern for cross-session memory persistence via structured markdown files (memory-bank/) that the agent is instructed to create, read, and update — a prompt-level (not deterministic) persistence approach, useful contrast for the kit's file-based working-state design.

results.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering (NeurIPS 2024)
results.snippet: Foundational citable result: harness/interface design materially changes agent performance. Prescribes compact action sets, built-in guardrails that prevent common mistakes, and concise deterministic feedback on every command — early evidence for deterministic verification inside the loop rather than relying on model behavior.

results.title: State of CLI Coding Agents, Mid-2026
results.snippet: Fresh mid-2026 comparative survey of CLI harnesses: which agents have persistent memory (Aider, Cline, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode) vs benchmark-only designs, and concrete choices like OpenCode persisting full session state (messages, tool outputs, costs) in SQLite for resumable sessions — useful current-practice snapshot, though an independent blog rather than primary source.

results.title: GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering (Zhipu AI technical report)
results.snippet: Primary-source technical report framing Zhipu's shift from 'vibe coding' to 'agentic engineering': sequential Reasoning->Agentic->General RL pipeline, asynchronous agent RL (Slime infrastructure), and long-horizon interaction training. The clearest Chinese-lab statement of how model-side training is expected to carry burden that Western harnesses put in prompts/instruction files — key evidence for the Western-vs-Chinese divergence analysis.

results.title: MiniMax Mini-Agent: minimal reference agent harness for MiniMax M2.x
results.snippet: MiniMax's own minimal-but-production-grade single-agent harness demo (Anthropic-compatible API, full interleaved-thinking support). A rare official Chinese-lab prescription for harness structure — tool loop, reasoning-state persistence across turns — directly comparable to Anthropic's Agent SDK / tinygrad-style minimal harness philosophy.

results.title: MiniMax: Interleaved Thinking Unlocks Reliable M2 Agentic Capability
results.snippet: Official guidance that harnesses must retain <think> blocks in message history across turns (removing them degrades performance; +3% SWE-Bench Verified, +40% BrowseComp). A concrete, citable Chinese-lab position on memory/working-state persistence in the harness — a divergence from harnesses that strip or compact reasoning.

results.title: MoonshotAI/Kimi-K2.5 — Agent Swarm and agentic model card
results.snippet: Moonshot's K2.5 repo documents Agent Swarm parallel orchestration (up to ~100 coordinated sub-agents, claimed 4.5x speedup) plus tool-use deployment guidance — the Chinese-lab counterpart to orchestrator/reduce and worktree-isolation multi-agent patterns, with model-native rather than harness-scripted parallelism.

results.title: Tencent Hunyuan officially releases Hy3, advancing agent capabilities
results.snippet: Official announcement of the July 2026 Hunyuan Hy3 launch (295B MoE, 21B active, Apache 2.0): claimed 90% task-completion in internal agent deployments, reasoning_effort modes, dedicated vLLM/SGLang tool-call parsers, and integration into the CodeBuddy coding assistant — covers the 'recent Hunyuan launch and agent tooling' item in the research question.

results.title: deepseek-ai/awesome-deepseek-agent — official DeepSeek agent integration index
results.snippet: DeepSeek's curated list of sanctioned agent harnesses and integrations for V4 (Claude Code, OpenCode, terminal agents), reflecting its strategy of shipping an Anthropic-compatible endpoint and reasoning-history conventions rather than its own governance layer — evidence that DeepSeek delegates instruction-file/enforcement practices to third-party harnesses.

claims.claim: Anthropic officially prescribes keeping CLAUDE.md short and aggressively pruned, warning that over-long instruction files cause the model to ignore instructions — the recommended test for each line is whether removing it would cause mistakes.
claims.quote: Keep it concise. For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!

claims.claim: Anthropic draws an explicit prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement line: CLAUDE.md instructions are advisory while hooks are deterministic, and hooks should be used for actions that must happen every time; a Stop hook can block turn completion until a check passes, with an override after 8 consecutive blocks.
claims.quote: Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.

claims.claim: Anthropic's top verification prescription is to give the agent a runnable pass/fail check (tests, build exit code, linter, screenshot diff) and offers an escalation ladder of gating strictness: in-prompt iteration, /goal conditions re-checked every turn, deterministic Stop hooks, and second-opinion verification subagents.
claims.quote: As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks.

claims.claim: For multi-agent orchestration, Anthropic recommends git-worktree-isolated parallel sessions, agent teams with a team lead, Writer/Reviewer session pairs, and adversarial review by a fresh-context subagent that sees only the diff and criteria — while warning that reviewers prompted to find gaps will over-report, causing over-engineering.
claims.quote: A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change, so it evaluates the result on its own terms.

claims.claim: For memory persistence across compaction, Anthropic recommends customizing compaction behavior via CLAUDE.md instructions (e.g., always preserving modified-file lists and test commands), plus locally persisted named sessions resumable with claude --continue/--resume as the cross-session memory mechanism.
claims.quote: Customize compaction behavior in CLAUDE.md with instructions like "When compacting, always preserve the full list of modified files and any test commands" to ensure critical context survives summarization

results.title: Ornith-1.0: Self-Scaffolding LLMs for Agentic Coding (DeepReinforce, June 2026)
results.snippet: VERIFIED: Ornith-1.0 is real — an MIT-licensed open coding model family (9B/31B dense, 35B/397B MoE, built on Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5) from DeepReinforce, released June 2026. Directly relevant to harness design: instead of human-designed harnesses, the model learns to generate its own task-specific RL scaffolds jointly with solutions; 397B variant reportedly matches Claude Opus 4.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Verified. Independent coverage exists (Simon Willison, MarkTechPost, Hugging Face repos), confirming this is not a hallucinated entity.

results.title: Don't rely on instructions, use Agent Hooks to enforce guardrails
results.snippet: Core of the prompt-vs-deterministic debate: argues everything in the context window (CLAUDE.md conventions, skills, prompts) is ultimately a suggestion whose compliance decays as sessions lengthen, while lifecycle hooks are deterministic enforcement executed by the runtime. Also notes agent hooks fire during the workflow, catching violations earlier than pre-commit hooks. Directly supports the 'prompts are guidance, hooks are guardrails' consensus a 2026 governance kit should encode.

results.title: Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses
results.snippet: Academic treatment of the repo's exact problem space: treating the coding-agent harness (instruction files, gates, hooks) as an engineered, observable artifact that evolves from telemetry rather than static prompt files — a citable 2026 reference for how harness/governance layers should be maintained and verified.

results.title: Hermes Agent | Nous Research
results.snippet: VERIFIED: The Nous Research 'Hermes agent' exists — an open-source, model-agnostic agent harness released Feb 2026 (v0.18.0 as of July 2026, GitHub: NousResearch/hermes-agent). Prescribes a distinctive memory model relevant to the persistence question: it autonomously distills skills from successful trajectories, persists user facts across sessions, and searches its own past conversations — an independent-lab counterpoint to Anthropic-style static CLAUDE.md memory.

results.title: George Hotz: AI Coding Agents Are a Disaster Waiting to Happen (Decrypt)
results.snippet: The minimal-harness skeptic position: after six months using agents on tinygrad, Hotz concluded output 'is broken in a way that's getting harder to detect' and agents 'frontload progress then give you a slot machine lever.' His radical-simplicity stance (tinygrad ~19k LOC) is the strongest argument that governance kits should bias toward deletion and hard verification gates over more prompt scaffolding; a community-made 'george-hotz-skills' Claude Code plugin codifies this as agent guidelines.

claims.claim: OpenAI Codex automatically loads project instruction files before starting any task: it reads AGENTS.md files as a mandatory pre-work step, making the instruction file the primary governance mechanism rather than an optional hint.
claims.quote: Codex reads `AGENTS.md` files before doing any work.

claims.claim: Codex resolves instruction files via a three-tier hierarchy — global (~/.codex, checking AGENTS.override.md then AGENTS.md), then project scope walking from the Git root down to the current directory — with at most one file loaded per directory and nested files taking precedence over ancestors.
claims.quote: Files closer to your current directory override earlier guidance

claims.claim: OpenAI imposes a hard deterministic size cap on combined instruction-file content: the default project_doc_max_bytes limit is 32 KiB, and Codex silently stops including additional AGENTS.md files once that budget is exhausted — the docs recommend splitting instructions across nested directories rather than one large file.
claims.quote: Codex stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit

claims.claim: Codex supports a dedicated override mechanism (AGENTS.override.md) checked before the base AGENTS.md at each scope, prescribed for temporary or localized rule changes placed 'as close to specialized work as possible' — a layered-override pattern for instruction governance.
claims.quote: Checks `AGENTS.override.md` first, then `AGENTS.md`

claims.claim: Instruction-file behavior is configurable through deterministic settings in ~/.codex/config.toml (project_doc_fallback_filenames for alternate names, project_doc_max_bytes for the size cap), and the page links to the standalone agents.md website, indicating AGENTS.md is positioned as a cross-tool open standard rather than a Codex-only convention.
claims.quote: The page references "the official [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md) website," suggesting broader adoption beyond Codex alone.

claims.claim: Gemini CLI loads GEMINI.md context files hierarchically in three tiers: a global file at ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, workspace files found in configured workspace directories and their parents, and just-in-time (JIT) files discovered when a tool touches a directory — meaning per-directory scoped instructions are a first-class mechanism, not a single monolithic file.
claims.quote: When a tool accesses a file or directory, the CLI automatically scans for `GEMINI.md` files in that directory and its ancestors up to a trusted root

claims.claim: Gemini CLI prescribes modularizing long instruction files via an @file.md import syntax rather than keeping one large file, explicitly to break down large GEMINI.md files into smaller components; imports support both relative and absolute paths.
claims.quote: both relative and absolute paths ... breaking down large `GEMINI.md` files into smaller, more manageable components

claims.claim: Gemini CLI natively supports AGENTS.md-style cross-vendor instruction files: the settings.json context.fileName property accepts an array of alternative filenames such as ["AGENTS.md", "CONTEXT.md", "GEMINI.md"], evidencing vendor convergence on the AGENTS.md convention.
claims.quote: The `settings.json` file's `context.fileName` property allows specifying alternative filenames: `["AGENTS.md", "CONTEXT.md", "GEMINI.md"]`

claims.claim: Gemini CLI exposes deterministic inspection and reload of the concatenated instruction context via /memory show and /memory reload commands, and surfaces the count of loaded context files in the CLI footer for visibility.
claims.quote: /memory show: "Displays the full, concatenated content of the current hierarchical memory" ... /memory reload: "Forces a re-scan and reload of all `GEMINI.md` files from all configured locations"

claims.claim: Google frames GEMINI.md files as carrying project-specific instructions, persona definitions, and coding style guides — i.e., behavioral/stylistic governance delivered via prompt-level instruction files rather than deterministic enforcement.
claims.quote: you can use these files to give project-specific instructions, define a persona, or provide coding style guides to make the AI's responses more accurate and tailored to your needs

claims.claim: AGENTS.md is an open, cross-vendor instruction-file format ('a README for agents') that has been adopted by over 60,000 open-source projects, making it the de facto standard rival/complement to CLAUDE.md-style project instruction files.
claims.quote: a dedicated, predictable place to provide the context and instructions to help AI coding agents work on your project ... used by over 60k open-source projects

claims.claim: AGENTS.md emerged from a collaboration including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google's Jules, Cursor, and Factory, and is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation — i.e., governance of the format itself has been formalized into a neutral foundation.
claims.quote: emerged from collaborative efforts across the AI software development ecosystem, including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules from Google, Cursor, and Factory ... now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation

claims.claim: The spec prescribes hierarchical instruction resolution: nested AGENTS.md files in monorepos, with the nearest file in the directory tree taking precedence, and cites OpenAI's main repo containing 88 AGENTS.md files as a real-world example.
claims.quote: Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence and every subproject can ship tailored instructions.

claims.claim: AGENTS.md ties instruction files to verification gating: agents are expected to execute programmatic checks listed in the file and fix failures before finishing a task.
claims.quote: Yes—if you list them. The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task.

claims.claim: The format deliberately imposes no schema or required fields — it is plain Markdown with free-form headings, meaning enforcement is prompt-based (the agent parses text) rather than deterministic/machine-validated.
claims.quote: AGENTS.md is just standard Markdown. Use any headings you like; the agent simply parses the text you provide.

claims.claim: Anthropic's Agent SDK exposes lifecycle hooks (including PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit) as callback functions that can deterministically validate, log, block, or transform agent behavior at defined points in the agent loop.
claims.quote: Run custom code at key points in the agent lifecycle. SDK hooks use callback functions to validate, log, block, or transform agent behavior. **Available hooks:** `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, and more.

claims.claim: Anthropic treats CLAUDE.md (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) as the memory/instruction-file mechanism for project context, loaded via filesystem-based configuration from .claude/ in the working directory and ~/.claude/, with a settingSources/setting_sources option to restrict which sources load.

claims.quote: Control exactly which tools your agent can use. Allow safe operations, block dangerous ones, or require approval for sensitive actions. ... This example creates a read-only agent that can analyze but not modify code. `allowed_tools` pre-approves `Read`, `Glob`, and `Grep`.

claims.claim: The SDK provides persistent session state across exchanges — sessions can be resumed by session ID or forked to explore alternatives, with session state stored as JSONL on the local filesystem (versus an Anthropic-hosted event log for Managed Agents).
claims.quote: Maintain context across multiple exchanges. Claude remembers files read, analysis done, and conversation history. Resume sessions later, or fork them to explore different approaches. ... **Session state** | JSONL on your filesystem | Anthropic-hosted event log

claims.quote: Target: fewer than 300 lines, with HumanLayer's own file being "less than sixty lines" ... Focus on universally applicable content only.

claims.quote: never let an agent write to `AGENTS.md` directly. The lead must approve every line.

claims.claim: Research cited in the article finds that LLM-generated AGENTS.md instruction files provide no benefit and can slightly hurt agent success rates while raising inference costs, implying instruction files should be human-authored and curated (the article says developer-written ones give a ~4% improvement).
claims.quote: LLM-generated AGENTS.md files offer no benefit and can marginally reduce success rates (~3% on average) while increasing inference costs by over 20%.

claims.claim: The article prescribes gatekeeping writes to the persistent instruction/memory file: agents must never write to AGENTS.md directly; a lead (human or orchestrator) must approve every line, while the file accumulates patterns across sessions as long-term memory.
claims.quote: Never let an agent write to `AGENTS.md` directly. The lead must approve every line.

claims.claim: Deterministic lifecycle hooks are recommended as verification gates in multi-agent setups — e.g. a TeammateIdle hook that blocks an agent from stopping until all tests pass — reflecting the article's thesis that 'the bottleneck is no longer generation. It's verification.'
claims.quote: A `TeammateIdle` hook verifies all tests pass before allowing an agent to stop working.

claims.claim: Cross-session/compaction memory persistence is achieved via multiple redundant deterministic channels: in the Ralph Loop pattern, git commit history, a progress log, a tasks.json state file, and AGENTS.md serve as the four persistence channels across context resets.
claims.quote: Four channels of memory persist across resets: git commit history, a progress log, the task state file (`tasks.json`), and `AGENTS.md` as long-term semantic memory.

claims.claim: For parallel multi-agent orchestration, git worktrees per agent are the standard isolation mechanism, and 3-5 parallel agents is the recommended team size, with token costs scaling linearly with team size and small focused agents outperforming one long-running generalist.
claims.quote: Git worktrees give each agent its own working directory. No merge conflicts while they work.

claims.claim: GitHub's Copilot desktop app isolates each parallel agent session in its own git worktree, making worktree isolation the concurrency-safety mechanism for multi-agent work.
claims.quote: Every session runs in its own git worktree, a real, isolated copy of your branch.

claims.claim: GitHub's cloud coding agent defaults to deterministic permission-gating on every write action, with fully autonomous 'autopilot' mode as an explicit opt-in after trust is established.
claims.quote: By default, the cloud agent asks permission before each write action. Switch to autopilot once you have established trust.

claims.claim: GitHub's 'Agent Merge' feature implements git-level enforcement of task completion conditions: the agent may drive CI back to green, address review feedback, and merge only when user-specified conditions are met.
claims.quote: Then Agent Merge helps carry that pull request through review, checks, and merge... You choose how far Copilot should go: drive CI back to green, address feedback, or merge when your conditions are met.

claims.claim: GitHub ships persistent cross-session, cross-surface agent memory as of mid-2026 via features named 'Memory++' and '/chronicle', spanning the desktop app, CLI, VS Code, and github.com.
claims.quote: Memory++ and `/chronicle` give Copilot continuity across devices and over time.

claims.claim: GitHub has productized adversarial multi-model review: the generally-available '/rubberduck' skill uses multiple model families to critique an implementation, and '/security-review' provides a dedicated security evaluation path.
claims.quote: The `/rubberduck` skill is now generally available to use multiple model families to critique your implementation and find novel issues.

claims.claim: ASDLC.io prescribes that adversarial review must run in a fresh, context-isolated session: the Critic agent should not share conversation history with the Builder, because accumulated context biases the review.
claims.quote: Start a new AI session or chat thread for critique. This clears conversation drift and forces the Critic to evaluate only the artifacts.

claims.claim: The pattern is motivated by a claimed failure mode called 'Self-Validation Ineffectiveness': an LLM asked to check code it just generated tends to assert correctness rather than find its own errors, justifying a separate reviewer agent instead of prompt-level self-review.
claims.quote: When asked 'Check your work,' a model that just generated code will often hallucinate correctness ... double down on errors.

claims.claim: For parallel multi-critic review, ASDLC.io prescribes a moderator/reduce layer that deduplicates and prioritizes findings so the Builder receives one consolidated fix list — an orchestrator/reduce pattern applied to adversarial review.
claims.quote: The moderator performs 'deduplication and prioritization,' ensuring 'the Builder agent receives a single, unified checklist of violations.'

claims.claim: The Review Gate implemented by this pattern is explicitly positioned as a middle tier between deterministic verification gates (compilers, tests) and subjective human acceptance gates, catching issues that 'Compilers miss...but that don't require human strategic judgment.'
claims.quote: Adversarial Code Review implements a Review Gate within the broader Context Gates architecture, positioned between 'deterministic' quality gates and subjective human acceptance gates.

claims.claim: The pattern assigns asymmetric model economics: cheap/fast models (named examples: Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5) as Builders optimizing throughput, with Critic agents given strict provenance/identity separation so their actions are audited independently; Critics emit binary PASS or an enumerated list of spec violations.
claims.quote: The Builder: 'Optimizes for implementation throughput (e.g., Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5).' ... Critics produce either 'PASS or a list of spec violations that must be addressed.'

claims.claim: Git worktree isolation for parallel coding agents converts silent mid-work file corruption into explicit merge-time git conflicts, which is the core rationale for using one worktree per agent.
claims.quote: Conflicts move to merge time, where standard git tooling detects them, instead of happening silently during active work.

claims.claim: Augment Code's Intent product implements a strict 1:1 mapping between a logical task workspace ('Space') and a dedicated git branch plus worktree, coordinated by a three-tier agent structure (Coordinator, six Specialist personas, and a Verifier agent acting as a quality gate).
claims.quote: When a developer creates a prompt in Intent, the application creates a Space with its own dedicated git branch and worktree.

claims.claim: The guide prescribes a deterministic verification-gate practice: establish a clean test baseline before the agent starts, then rerun the suite after, so failures can be attributed to the agent's changes.
claims.quote: The most valuable practice is establishing a clean test baseline before the agent starts work.

claims.claim: Worktree isolation alone is insufficient for parallel agents: it isolates files but not runtime resources (ports, databases, caches, test state), so supplementary runtime isolation (e.g., Docker, deterministic port assignment by branch-name hashing into the 3100-9999 range) is required.
claims.quote: worktree isolation stops one task from trampling another's files, but does not stop one task's runtime from trampling another's ports, databases, caches, secrets, or test state

claims.claim: As of 2026, running roughly four or five Claude agents simultaneously per developer is presented as a realistic operating scale for worktree-based parallelism, with worktree creation cheaper than cloning because the object store is shared.
claims.quote: Storage cost scales with working file count, not repository history size. Creating a worktree is often faster than cloning

claims.claim: An adversarial, stage-gated multi-agent review pipeline (Refute-or-Promote) killed roughly 79% of ~171 defect candidates before disclosure over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets, with an 83% prospective kill rate on a consolidated-protocol subset (n=30), demonstrating that most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives that structured adversarial gating can filter out.
claims.quote: Over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets (security libraries, the ISO C++ standard, major compilers), the pipeline killed ∼79% of ∼171 candidates before advancing to disclosure (retrospective aggregate); on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n = 30), the prospective kill rate was 83%.

claims.claim: Unanimous multi-agent consensus is not evidence of correctness: 80+ agents (including ten dedicated adversarial reviewers) unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module, and only a single empirical test killed it — motivating a mandatory deterministic empirical validation gate rather than prompt-level consensus as the final arbiter.
claims.quote: ten dedicated reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL’s CMS module; it was killed only by a single empirical test, motivating the mandatory empirical gate.

claims.claim: A Cross-Model Critic — an agent from a different model family given minimal context — catches correlated training-data errors that same-family review misses: in the libfuse campaign it found correctness errors in 3 of 19 (~16%) fixes that same-family review had approved, and surfaced 3 additional bugs same-family review missed.
claims.quote: In the libfuse campaign specifically, CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (∼16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes and independently surfaced 3 bugs that same-family review had missed

claims.claim: Deliberate context asymmetry is prescribed as an anti-anchoring mechanism in multi-agent review: adversarial reviewer agents are given only the candidate claim, withholding the proposing agent's reasoning, so cold-start reviewers cannot anchor on the advocate's framing.
claims.quote: adversarial agents receive only the candidate claim, not the creative agent’s reasoning, preventing anchoring on the advocate’s framing.

claims.claim: The methodology's governance artifacts are codified as persistent instruction files — 56 refute-or-promote rules plus a 'strat.md' orchestration playbook — which transferred directly to a structurally similar codebase (wolfSSL); a simplified cross-family-critique variant also solved 5 SWE-bench Verified SymPy instances where all 134 publicly-logged prior submissions had failed, suggesting the pattern transfers from defect discovery to general coding-agent tasks.
claims.quote: our 56 rules transferred directly to a structurally similar codebase (wolfSSL), appearing to improve precision before that campaign’s first failure. ... The variant produced 5 verified SymPy fixes, plus a 914-byte patch for the “hardest task” on swe-rebench.com (Nov–Dec 2025).

claims.claim: The article defines the 'harness' as everything in an AI coding agent except the model itself, formalizing 'Agent = Model + Harness' as the framing for harness engineering — the same problem space as the claude.md-workflow repo.
claims.quote: The term harness has emerged as a shorthand to mean everything in an AI agent except the model itself - Agent = Model + Harness.

claims.claim: It prescribes a control-systems taxonomy for governance mechanisms: feedforward 'guides' (e.g. AGENTS.md instruction files, which steer the agent before it acts) versus feedback 'sensors' (checks that observe after the agent acts and enable self-correction).
claims.quote: Guides (feedforward controls) - anticipate the agent's behaviour and aim to steer it before it acts. Sensors (feedback controls) - observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct.

claims.claim: It explicitly distinguishes deterministic ('computational') enforcement — linters, type checkers, tests, run by CPU — from non-deterministic ('inferential') enforcement such as LLM code review / LLM-as-judge, recommending computational sensors for reliable enforcement and inferential ones only for semantic judgment. This directly supports the prompt-vs-deterministic-enforcement axis of the research question.
claims.quote: Computational - deterministic and fast, run by the CPU. Inferential - Semantic analysis, AI code review, 'LLM as judge'. Typically run by a GPU or NPU.

claims.claim: It prescribes shift-left placement of verification gates in the agent lifecycle: fast, cheap checks (linters, basic review agents) before integration, expensive checks (mutation testing, broad code review) after, because earlier detection is cheaper.
claims.quote: You want to have checks as far left in the path to production as possible, since the earlier you find issues, the cheaper they are to fix.

claims.claim: It proposes 'harness templates' — pre-packaged bundles of guides and sensors tied to a service topology (CRUD service, dashboard, event processor) — as a future drop-in governance-kit pattern, plus continuous out-of-lifecycle drift sensors (dead code, coverage quality, dependency scanning); notably it does NOT prescribe instruction-file length/structure, memory persistence, scope-creep guardrails, task contracts, or concrete multi-agent/worktree architectures.
claims.quote: These might evolve into harness templates in the future: a bundle of guides and sensors that leash a coding agent to the structure, conventions and tech stack of a topology.

claims.claim: OpenHands SDK ships an LLM-based summarizing condenser as its default mechanism for handling context growth, meaning the flagship open-source coding harness relies on model-generated summaries (not raw truncation) for compaction.
claims.quote: OpenHands SDK provides `LLMSummarizingCondenser` as the default condenser implementation.

claims.claim: OpenHands' condensation is triggered deterministically by an event-count threshold and always pins the earliest events (system prompt and initial user message), a concrete design pattern for preserving project instructions across compaction.
claims.quote: This condenser triggers when there are more than `max_context_length` events in the conversation history, and always keeps the first `keep_first` events (system prompts, initial user messages) to preserve important context.

claims.claim: When the threshold is exceeded, OpenHands replaces dropped conversation events with a single LLM-generated summary rather than deleting them silently; configuration is via max_size and keep_first parameters (documented example: max_size=10, keep_first=2).
claims.quote: The condenser will automatically truncate conversation history when it exceeds max_size, and replaces the dropped events with an LLM-generated summary.

claims.claim: OpenHands claims its summarizing condensation cuts per-turn API costs by up to 2x, a checkable efficiency figure relevant to whether governance kits should recommend summary-based compaction over full-history retention.
claims.quote: Up to **2x reduction** in per-turn API costs

claims.claim: The condenser is built as an extensible class hierarchy (LLMSummarizingCondenser extends RollingCondenser extends a condenser base), and the docs' example shows condenser state persisting across sessions via conversation serialization to a ./.conversations directory.
claims.quote: `LLMSummarizingCondenser` extends `RollingCondenser`, which itself extends `CondenserBase`, enabling custom implementations while leveraging SDK conversation management infrastructure.

claims.claim: Cline's Memory Bank prescribes a hierarchical set of six markdown files as persistent agent memory (projectbrief.md, productContext.md, systemPatterns.md, techContext.md, activeContext.md, progress.md), with projectbrief.md as the root source of truth from which the others derive.
claims.quote: projectbrief.md is the source of truth from which other docs come from

claims.claim: Memory Bank mandates a deterministic lifecycle: the agent must read all memory files and verify context completeness before starting work, then update the relevant docs and ensure cross-file consistency after every change — a read/verify/execute/update loop enforced via custom instructions.
claims.quote: Before work begins, Cline must "Read all Memory Bank files" and "Verify context is complete." After changes, it should "Update relevant documentation" and "Ensure consistency across files."

claims.claim: Cline justifies file-based memory persistence by finite context windows (cited as 32k–200k tokens as of Feb 2025), arguing that when context fills, users face losing context, manual prompt management, or lossy summarization — motivating on-disk memory that survives session resets and compaction.
claims.quote: AI assistants operate with finite "context window" capacity—"typically ranging from 32k to 200k tokens."

claims.claim: The Memory Bank instruction file embeds Mermaid flowcharts inside the custom instructions to teach the agent its documentation-maintenance workflow, i.e., using visual/diagrammatic structure rather than prose-only instruction files.
claims.quote: combining "visual flowcharts to teach the AI how to maintain text documentation."

claims.claim: Session recovery works by cold-start rehydration: after any context reset, the agent rebuilds project understanding purely by re-reading the memory files, eliminating the need for the user to re-explain project, tech stack, and architecture each session.
claims.quote: Memory Bank solves this by letting Cline "quickly rebuild its understanding by reading these files" when sessions restart.

claims.claim: Persistent memory implementation cleanly divides benchmark-oriented from interactive coding agents: of the 13 analyzed scaffolds, the five CLI agents built for interactive use (Aider, Cline, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode) implement cross-session persistence, while five benchmark/research agents (SWE-agent, OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, mini-swe-agent, DARS-Agent) have none.
claims.quote: All five agents with no persistent memory (SWE-agent, OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, mini-swe-agent, DARS-Agent) treat each task as independent, with no cross-task learning... The five CLI agents with persistent memory (Aider, Cline, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode) target interactive development where remembering project conventions and past decisions has direct value.

claims.claim: A distinct 'LLM as memory author' pattern exists in which the agent writes its own persistent instruction files: Cline's new_rule tool creates .clinerules files, Gemini CLI's save_memory tool appends to GEMINI.md (with @path/to/file composition), while Codex CLI instead uses a background two-phase pipeline (extraction with gpt-5.1-codex-mini, consolidation via a gpt-5.3-codex sub-agent, usage-ranked with stale-memory pruning) that consolidates memories without the LLM explicitly deciding what to remember.
claims.quote: Cline and Gemini CLI share a pattern where the LLM writes its own persistent instructions. Cline's new rule tool creates .clinerules files; Gemini CLI's save memory tool appends to GEMINI.md... Codex CLI takes a different approach: a background pipeline extracts and consolidates memories without the LLM explicitly deciding what to remember.

claims.claim: Project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style) are becoming a cross-vendor interoperability layer: Cline reads not only its own .clinerules/ but also .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, and AGENTS.md, and the paper distinguishes such static, user-written configuration from true persistent memory because the agent never writes or updates it.
claims.quote: Cline reads not only its own .clinerules/ but also .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, and AGENTS.md. This pragmatic interoperability reflects an emerging ecosystem where developers use multiple AI coding tools with shared project-level instructions [Galster et al., 2026].

claims.claim: Evidence favors deterministic scaffold-level verification over prompt-based enforcement: the paper cites Chen et al. (2026) finding that prompt interventions adding or removing testing change SWE-bench outcomes by at most 2.6 percentage points, concluding that scaffold-orchestrated testing (lint-test cycles, test-gated retries, MCTS reward signals) rather than model-native test-writing behavior is the architecturally relevant variable.
claims.quote: Chen et al. [2026] examine whether agent-generated tests improve resolution rates under a minimal scaffold, finding that prompt interventions that add or remove testing change outcomes by at most 2.6 percentage points; this suggests that scaffold-level orchestration of testing (lint-test cycles, test-gated retries, MCTS reward signals), rather than model-native test-writing behavior, may be the architecturally relevant variable.

claims.claim: Behavioral guardrails in production agents range from structural (deterministic) to LLM-judged: Prometheus binds different tool subsets to different graph nodes as 'structural guardrailing', while Codex CLI is the only agent in the 13-agent corpus that uses a separate LLM (a Guardian safety subagent running gpt-5.4) to score each tool call's risk on a 0-100 scale and block calls above 80 — and the paper concludes no standard safety/isolation approach has emerged for interactive agents.
claims.quote: a Guardian safety subagent, a separate LLM (gpt-5.4), evaluates each tool call's risk with structured scoring on a 0–100 scale, blocking calls above a threshold of 80 (guardian.rs). This is the only agent in the corpus that uses an LLM to evaluate the safety of another LLM's actions.

claims.claim: Zhipu AI explicitly frames GLM-5 as a paradigm shift from 'vibe coding' to 'agentic engineering', i.e., positioning the model for autonomous end-to-end software engineering rather than interactive assisted coding.
claims.quote: We present GLM-5, a next-generation foundation model designed to transition the paradigm of vibe coding to agentic engineering.

claims.claim: GLM-5's agentic capability is trained via a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that decouples generation from training, plus novel asynchronous agent RL algorithms for long-horizon interactions — indicating Zhipu invests in model-side RL training for agency rather than harness-side scaffolding.
claims.quote: we implement a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupling generation from training. Furthermore, we propose novel asynchronous agent RL algorithms that further improve RL quality, enabling the model to learn from complex, long-horizon interactions more effectively.

claims.claim: GLM-5 adopts DSA (sparse attention) to cut training/inference cost while preserving long-context fidelity — relevant to how Chinese labs handle long-context persistence needed by coding agents.
claims.quote: Building upon the agentic, reasoning, and coding (ARC) capabilities of its predecessor, GLM-5 adopts DSA to significantly reduce training and inference costs while maintaining long-context fidelity.

claims.claim: Zhipu claims GLM-5 achieves state-of-the-art results on major open benchmarks and surpasses prior baselines on end-to-end real-world software engineering tasks — a checkable benchmark claim.
claims.quote: GLM-5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on major open benchmarks. Most critically, GLM-5 demonstrates unprecedented capability in real-world coding tasks, surpassing previous baselines in handling end-to-end software engineering challenges.

claims.claim: The GLM-5 technical report exists as arXiv 2602.15763, authored by the GLM-5 Team (185 authors including Aohan Zeng, Xin Lv, Zhenyu Hou, Zhengxiao Du), submitted 2026-02-17 and revised 2026-02-24 — confirming the named entity 'GLM-5' is verifiable.
claims.quote: Lead Authors: GLM-5-Team including Aohan Zeng, Xin Lv, Zhenyu Hou, Zhengxiao Du, and 184 additional authors (185 total) ... Submitted: February 17, 2026 (v1)

claims.claim: SWE-agent (Princeton, NeurIPS 2024) establishes four agent-computer interface (ACI) design principles, the fourth being that deterministic guardrails (e.g., automatic syntax checking) mitigate error propagation and speed agent recovery — a direct precedent for deterministic verification gates over prompt-only enforcement.
claims.quote: Guardrails mitigate error propagation and hasten recovery. Like humans, LMs make mistakes when editing or searching and can struggle to recover from these errors. Building in guardrails, such as a code syntax checker that automatically detects mistakes, can help agents recognize and quickly correct errors.

claims.claim: A deterministic lint gate (flake8 with selected syntax error codes) that reverts any edit introducing a syntax error improved SWE-bench Lite resolution from 15.0% to 18.0% in ablation — i.e., removing the linting guardrail cost 3.0 absolute points.
claims.quote: we add an intervention to the edit logic that lets a modification apply only if it does not produce major errors. We compare this interface with the No edit and edit w/o linting alternatives in Figure 6. This intervention improves performance considerably (without linting, 15.0% ↓ 3.0 ).

claims.claim: SWE-agent manages context by collapsing all but the 5 most recent observations to a single line each — an early, quantified precedent for compaction/working-state management in coding-agent harnesses.
claims.quote: observations preceding the last 5 are each collapsed into a single line, shown in Figure 31. By removing most content from prior observations, we maintain essential information about the plan and action history while reducing unnecessary context, which allows for more interaction cycles and avoids showing outdated file information.

claims.claim: Harness design alone (LM held constant at GPT-4 Turbo) produced a 64% relative improvement over a plain Linux-shell agent and a 6.7x improvement over non-interactive RAG on SWE-bench, with SWE-agent solving 12.47% of the full test set — evidence that interface/harness engineering, not just model capability, drives coding-agent performance.
claims.quote: compared to RAG on Lite, SWE-agent is 8-13x more costly but yields a 6.7-fold improved % Resolved rate. An LM-friendly ACI's value is confirmed by SWE-agent's 64% relative increase compared to Shell-only, both with GPT-4 Turbo.

claims.claim: Agents are sensitive to observation window size: showing 100 lines of a file was optimal, while showing only 30 lines (14.3%, down 3.7) or the entire file (12.7%, down 5.3) both hurt SWE-bench Lite performance — supporting bounded, curated context over maximal context in harness design.
claims.quote: We also find that agents are sensitive to the number of lines the file viewer displays. Either too little content (30 lines, 14.3% ↓ 3.7 ) or too much (entire file, 12.7% ↓ 5.3 ) lowers performance.

claims.claim: MiniMax publishes Mini-Agent as an official minimal reference harness demonstrating its recommended best practices for building coding/general agents on the MiniMax M2.5 model, positioning a deliberately small, readable codebase as the intended starting point for advanced agents.
claims.quote: a minimal yet professional demo project that showcases the best practices for building agents with the MiniMax M2.5 model... Clean & Simple Design: A beautiful CLI and a codebase that is easy to understand, making it the perfect starting point for building advanced agents.

claims.claim: Mini-Agent handles persistent agent memory across sessions via a dedicated Session Note Tool, rather than relying solely on the context window or instruction files.
claims.quote: Session Note Tool ensures "the agent retains key information across multiple sessions"

claims.claim: Mini-Agent manages long-context degradation through automatic conversation-history summarization up to a configurable token limit (i.e., built-in compaction in the harness rather than manual context management).
claims.quote: Intelligent context management that "automatically summarizes conversation history to handle contexts up to a configurable token limit"

claims.claim: MiniMax's harness adopts Anthropic-ecosystem conventions: it uses an Anthropic-compatible API with interleaved thinking and integrates Claude Skills (a bundle of 15 professional skills) plus MCP tools — evidence of Chinese-lab convergence on Anthropic's agent interface standards.
claims.quote: demonstrates agent architecture using an Anthropic-compatible API with interleaved thinking support... The repository references "Claude Skills" (15 professional skills)... MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool integration for knowledge graphs and web search

claims.claim: Mini-Agent is MIT-licensed, Python-based (~91% Python), single-agent in scope (execution loop + file system and shell toolset), with no documented multi-agent orchestration or deterministic verification gates in its README.
claims.quote: Complete execution loop with basic toolset for file system and shell operations... MIT License... Primary language is Python (90.9%)

claims.claim: MiniMax defines and prescribes 'interleaved thinking' — alternating explicit reasoning with tool calls while carrying reasoning forward between steps — as the mechanism for reliable long-horizon agentic behavior in M2, a design position directly relevant to harness memory/state persistence across turns.
claims.quote: Interleaved thinking means alternating between explicit reasoning and tool use, while carrying that reasoning forward between steps.

claims.claim: MiniMax reports concrete benchmark degradation when prior-round reasoning state is dropped: preserving reasoning state yields 69.4 vs 67.2 on SWE-Bench Verified, 87 vs 64 on Tau², 44.0 vs 31.4 on BrowseComp, 75.7 vs 67.9 on GAIA, and 72.0 vs 66.0 on xBench.
claims.quote: SWE‑Bench Verified: 69.4 vs. 67.2 (+3.3%); Tau²: 87 vs. 64 (+35.9%); BrowseComp: 44.0 vs. 31.4 (+40.1%)

claims.claim: MiniMax prescribes a concrete harness-level requirement for M2: developers must pass the reasoning_details field back into subsequent requests so the model retains its chain of thought across multi-turn tool use — i.e., state persistence is delegated to the client harness, not the model.
claims.quote: Passing the reasoning_details field in subsequent requests ensures that the model maintains a complete chain of thought across multiple tool calls.

claims.claim: MiniMax claims that dropping prior reasoning state causes measurable failure modes in agent loops — state drift, weakened self-correction, and degraded planning — framing prompt-context continuity as a reliability requirement rather than an optimization.
claims.quote: When prior state is dropped, cumulative understanding breaks down, state drift increases, self‑correction weakens, and planning degrades.

claims.claim: MiniMax states the standard OpenAI Chat Completions API is incompatible with its interleaved-thinking workflow because it cannot return reasoning content in subsequent requests, so developers must use MiniMax's OpenAI-Compatible or Anthropic-Compatible endpoints — a notable interoperability divergence for harness builders.
claims.quote: does not support passing reasoning content back in subsequent requests

claims.claim: Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5 implements multi-agent orchestration at the model level via 'Agent Swarm': the model itself decomposes tasks and dynamically instantiates parallel domain-specific sub-agents, rather than relying on a harness-defined orchestrator/reduce pattern.
claims.quote: K2.5 transitions from single-agent scaling to a self-directed, coordinated swarm-like execution scheme. It decomposes complex tasks into parallel sub-tasks executed by dynamically instantiated, domain-specific agents.

claims.claim: Moonshot prescribes a specific first-party harness pairing for coding work — the model card explicitly states K2.5 performs best inside Kimi Code CLI, indicating a co-designed model+harness approach rather than harness-agnostic deployment.
claims.quote: Kimi K2.5 works best with Kimi Code CLI as its agent framework — give it a try at https://www.kimi.com/code.

claims.claim: Kimi K2.5's Agent Swarm mode measurably outperforms its own single-agent mode on agentic search benchmarks (BrowseComp 78.4% swarm vs 60.6% base; WideSearch 79.0% vs 72.7%), with swarm runs bounded by explicit step budgets (main agent max 15 steps, sub-agents max 100 steps on BrowseComp).
claims.quote: BrowseComp (Swarm Mode): main agent max 15 steps; sub-agents max 100 steps. WideSearch (Swarm Mode): main and sub-agents max 100 steps.

claims.claim: K2.5 (Thinking mode) scores 76.8% on SWE-Bench Verified (averaged over 5 independent runs), placing a Chinese open-weights MoE model (1T total / 32B active params, 256K context) in the frontier tier for autonomous coding-agent capability as of its release.
claims.quote: SWE-Bench Verified: 76.8 ... all reported scores of coding tasks are averaged over 5 independent runs.

claims.claim: K2.5's agentic execution model is built on interleaved reasoning with multi-step tool calls (inherited from K2 Thinking), with deployment-level determinism guidance limited to sampling settings (temperature 1.0 thinking / 0.6 instant, top_p 0.95) — the model card prescribes nothing about instruction files, memory persistence, or verification gates, leaving those to the harness.
claims.quote: K2.5 shares the same design of Interleaved Thinking and Multi-Step Tool Call as K2 Thinking. ... The recommended temperature will be 1.0 for Thinking mode and 0.6 for Instant mode. The recommended top_p is 0.95.

claims.claim: Instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) are unreliably followed by coding agents — the author reports that a rule written in CLAUDE.md (e.g., always use a design-system component instead of a raw <input>) is ignored by the agent roughly half the time, motivating deterministic enforcement instead.
claims.quote: Just writing 'always use `<.cinput>`, never raw `<input>`' in CLAUDE.md. That's the exact thing the agent ignores half the time

claims.claim: Agent lifecycle hooks provide deterministic, 100%-firing enforcement in contrast to probabilistic prompt-based instructions, and this is presented as the reason to prefer hooks over emphatic instruction-file language.
claims.quote: Both deterministic, both fire every single time and give you more confidence that the agent isn't going sideways by ignoring your MUST DO VERY IMPORTANT DON'T FORGET instructions.

claims.claim: In Claude Code's hook system, the PreToolUse hook is the point where a tool call can actually be blocked, and blocking depends on the exit code: exit 2 blocks the tool while exit 1 only logs a warning and lets the tool through.
claims.quote: fires right before Claude Code runs a tool, and it's the one place where you can actually stop the tool from happening by exiting with an error code ... Exit `1` only logs a warning and lets the tool through

claims.claim: The Stop hook fires when the agent declares itself finished, and exiting with code 2 plus a stderr message forces the agent to keep working — usable as a deterministic completion gate (e.g., never accept 'done' while a design-system ratchet test fails).
claims.quote: Exit `2` here means 'no, keep working,' and the stderr message tells it why.

claims.claim: Running verification via a PostToolUse hook after every edit is workable but suboptimal, because it fires constantly on legitimately half-finished code, making it slow and noisy — an argument for gating at Stop/completion time rather than per-edit.
claims.quote: A `PostToolUse` hook running the ratchet after every edit. It works, but it fires constantly mid-task when the code is legitimately half-finished, so it's slow and noisy.

result.summary: As of July 2026, coding-agent governance has converged on a clear architecture across Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub/Microsoft: short, hierarchical, nearest-file-wins instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, the latter now a Linux Foundation-stewarded cross-vendor standard used by 60k+ projects); an explicit split between advisory prompt-level instructions and deterministic harness-level enforcement (lifecycle hooks, permission gates, Stop-hook verification gates); runnable pass/fail checks as the primary quality mechanism with an escalation ladder from in-prompt iteration to hard gates; and git-worktree isolation as the standard concurrency-safety mechanism for parallel multi-agent work. Adversarial-review research (Refute-or-Promote, arXiv 2604.19049) supplies the strongest citable warning: 80+ agents unanimously endorsed a non-existent OpenSSL vulnerability that only an empirical test killed, so consensus and LLM review must be subordinate to deterministic empirical validation, ideally with a cross-model critic to break correlated blind spots. The one verified non-Western data point (Zhipu's GLM-5) shows a divergent bet on model-side asynchronous agent RL rather than harness-side scaffolding. For a 2026 governance-kit rewrite, the actionable prescriptions are: aggressively prune instruction files (Anthropic's removal test; OpenAI's 32 KiB hard cap), split guidance into nested per-directory files, move every must-happen rule from prose into hooks/permission gates, gate task completion on executable checks rather than agent self-report or reviewer consensus, and isolate parallel agents in worktrees with fresh-context, diff-only adversarial reviewers whose findings are treated as noisy signals, not mandates.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus: instruction files must be short, and vendors now enforce or prescribe brevity. Anthropic officially instructs users to aggressively prune CLAUDE.md — the test for each line is 'would removing this cause mistakes?' — warning that bloated files cause the model to ignore instructions. OpenAI enforces the same principle deterministically: Codex caps combined AGENTS.md content at 32 KiB by default (project_doc_max_bytes) and silently stops loading files beyond it, with docs recommending splitting instructions across nested directories rather than growing one file.

Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!' OpenAI (verbatim): 'Codex stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit' (32 KiB default); silent truncation corroborated by openai/codex issue #7138. Both are live primary vendor docs fetched 2026-07-14.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus: hierarchical, nearest-file-wins instruction resolution is the standard structure. Codex resolves instructions via global scope (~/.codex, AGENTS.override.md then AGENTS.md) followed by a walk from Git root to cwd, at most one file per directory, nested files overriding ancestors. The AGENTS.md spec prescribes the same for monorepos — nested per-package files with nearest-file precedence — citing OpenAI's main repo containing 88 AGENTS.md files as a real-world example.

findings.claim: AGENTS.md has become the de facto cross-vendor instruction-file standard with formalized neutral governance: it emerged from OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google's Jules, Cursor, and Factory, is used by over 60,000 open-source projects (verifier's independent GitHub search found ~158k matching files, so the figure is conservative), and is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation (announced Dec 2025 alongside Anthropic's MCP donation). Codex treats it as the primary governance mechanism, automatically reading AGENTS.md files before doing any work — though loading is mandatory while compliance remains prompt-level and advisory.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement: every major Western vendor draws an explicit line between advisory prompt instructions and deterministic harness enforcement, and prescribes moving must-happen rules to the harness. Anthropic states CLAUDE.md is advisory while hooks are deterministic ('use hooks for actions that must happen every time'); a Stop hook can block turn completion until a check passes (overridden after 8 consecutive blocks). The Agent SDK exposes lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit) as callbacks that validate, log, block, or transform behavior, plus a deterministic permissions system (allowed_tools pre-approval, e.g. a read-only agent limited to Read/Glob/Grep). GitHub's cloud agent defaults to permission-gating every write action, with autonomous 'autopilot' as explicit opt-in after trust is established.

GitHub verbatim: 'By default, the cloud agent asks permission before each write action. Switch to autopilot once you have established trust.' findings.claim: Convergent consensus on verification gating: the top prescription across vendors is a runnable pass/fail check as the arbiter of completion, with an escalation ladder of strictness. Anthropic's lead best practice is giving the agent a verifiable check (tests, build exit code, linter, screenshot diff) and choosing how hard it gates: in-prompt iteration → /goal conditions re-checked every turn → deterministic Stop hooks → second-opinion verification subagents. The AGENTS.md spec ties instruction files to the same expectation: agents execute programmatic checks listed in the file and fix failures before finishing. GitHub's Agent Merge extends gating to the git level: the agent drives CI back to green, addresses review feedback, and merges only when user-specified conditions are met.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on multi-agent orchestration: git-worktree isolation is the industry-standard concurrency-safety mechanism, and orchestrator/subagent patterns are first-class. Anthropic recommends worktree-isolated parallel sessions, agent teams with a team lead, and Writer/Reviewer session pairs; its Agent SDK supports subagents with specialized instructions and restricted tool lists, invoked via an Agent tool, with parent_tool_use_id attribution per subagent execution. GitHub's Copilot desktop app independently converged on the same design: every parallel agent session runs in its own git worktree, managed automatically.

GitHub verbatim: 'Every session runs in its own git worktree, a real, isolated copy of your branch.' SDK docs confirm AgentDefinition (prompt + tools restriction) and parent_tool_use_id verbatim. findings.claim: Adversarial review works but has sharply documented limits, yielding three citable design rules. (1) Reviewer over-reporting: Anthropic warns that a reviewer prompted to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound, and chasing every finding causes over-engineering; its prescribed mitigation is a fresh-context subagent that sees only the diff and criteria. (2) Consensus is not correctness: in the Refute-or-Promote study, 80+ agents including ten dedicated adversarial reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module; only a single empirical test killed it — motivating a mandatory deterministic empirical-validation gate rather than prompt-level consensus as final arbiter. (3) Cross-model critique breaks correlated blind spots: a critic from a different model family found correctness errors in 3 of 19 (~16%) fixes that same-family review had approved, plus 3 additional missed bugs, in the libfuse campaign.

Anthropic treats CLAUDE.md/.claude/CLAUDE.md as the project memory/instruction mechanism, loaded via filesystem configuration (.claude/ and ~/.claude/, restrictable via settingSources); its SDK persists session state as local JSONL, resumable by session ID or forkable to explore alternatives (versus an Anthropic-hosted event log for Managed Agents).
